title: Self‑hosted Forces and Fallback Strategy
content:
Purpose:
This brief is a tactical GTM note for sales and product marketing to quickly explain where self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM flavors and bespoke deployments) make sense, where they fail, and the practical fallback/escape-hatch messaging we should use to convert deal risk into Redwood differentiation.

Audience:
- Sales reps engaging infra/platform buyers
- Solutions engineers prepping discovery 
- Product marketing for short battlecards and objection responses

TL;DR (30s):
Many engineering teams start evaluating self-hosted runtimes because they believe it will be cheaper or more controllable. In reality there are three major regimes: exploratory/PoC, steady-state at moderate scale, and high-throughput/enterprise. Self-hosted can look attractive in the first two but fails on operational overhead, unpredictable SLOs, and regression risk at scale. Redwood wins when we position as a predictable control-plane with escape hatches: start hosted, then scale to Dedicated or Private with preserved API contracts and rollout tooling.

Key buyer questions and succinct answers (ready-to-say lines):
- "Can we run everything ourselves to save costs?" -> Running yourself can reduce unit compute cost on paper but introduces hidden operator tax: engineering time, incident drag, patching/compat, model ops, and tail-latency debugging. Redwood captures most of the upside without the tax and with clear migration lanes.
- "Why not just vLLM + fast hardware?" -> vLLM gives fast token paths but lacks the orchestration, autoscaling, and multi-tenant safety nets. You still need caching layers, rollout tooling, and quality monitoring — all of which we provide.
- "What about TGI or Triton/TensorRT stacks?" -> TGI/Triton offer performance wins for certain model families but they require significant infra engineering to maintain kernel selection, quantization knobs, and version rollouts. Our runtime automates kernel selection and model variants, reducing long-term maintenance.

Operator cost taxonomy (practical list for discovery):
- One-time engineering setup: infra provisioning, CI/CD, image management
- Ongoing ops: patching, kernel upgrades, runtime tuning, quantization regressions
- Incident cost: debugging tail-latency, memory fragmentation, KV cache corruption
- Quality risk: drift/regression when swapping quantized or optimized variants
- Hidden infra: network egress, cold-start waste, capacity fragmentation

Competitive technical comparison (high level):
- vLLM: great for research and small fleets; low barrier to entry; high maintenance to get multi-tenant reliability and autoscaling right.
- TGI (Text Generation Inference): strong for Hugging Face model families and direct Torch integration; needs ops glue for large-scale inference farms.
- TensorRT-LLM / Triton combos: best for latency-sensitive, highly-optimized quantized models on Nvidia fleets; high performance but brittle upgrades and more vendor lock-in.

Decision triggers we recommend qualifying in discovery (yes/no checklist):
- Is the team willing to allocate >1 FTE for inference ops for the next 12 months?
- Do they have strict on-prem or regulatory constraints that preclude managed control planes?
- Is predictable token cost per unit more important than minimizing peak latency at any cost?
- Are they planning frequent model rollouts / A/B tests / canary deployments?
If buyer answers NO to the first and/or YES to the last two, push Redwood hosted/Dedicated.

Cost regimes and example narratives (verbal scripts for AE/SE):
- Small PoC (1-2 nodes): "Self-hosted looks cheaper but you’ll spend cycles rebuilding observability and rollout tooling. Host with us to validate product-market fit, then we’ll help you map a Dedicated contract if you need capacity guarantees."
- Mid-scale (10s of GPUs): "At this size operator burden becomes visible — our cost advisory can show you the point where Managed + Reserved capacity reduces TCO once you include SRE/eng time."
- High-scale (100s+ GPUs): "You likely need a platform team; Redwood’s Dedicated and Private options are designed to replace brittle bespoke fleets while keeping you in control of model versioning and data locality."

Failure modes to call out in-discussion (concrete examples):
- Silent regression: quantization introduced a subtle failure in hallucination rate after a kernel upgrade — took weeks to find.
- Capacity blackhole: misconfigured autoscale policies cause cascading OOMs during burst queries.
- Fragmented latency: heterogeneous hardware + different quantization leads to unpredictable p99s across endpoints.
These are where a managed control plane with regression alerts and canary rollouts delivers direct value.

Redwood positioning pillars to emphasize (short phrases):
- "Predictable economics, not just lower sticker price."
- "Preserve control, remove toil."
- "Migration-safe: same API, evolving infra."

Objections and rebuttals (quick bullets):
- "We need full control for compliance" -> Offer Private deployment narrative + KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs; propose an on-prem evaluation with limited scope.
- "Managed is a single point of failure" -> Explain multi-tier routing and fallback policies (region, model variants) and SLA commitments; highlight customer examples.
- "We can squeeze more performance ourselves" -> Acknowledge micro-optimizations but contrast long-term maintenance and regression risk; offer a cost/perf audit comparing their telemetry to our benchmarks.

Suggested sales plays and collateral mapping:
- PoC play: "Start hosted, prove the feature, then reserve Dedicated capacity." (Collateral: 1-pager, cost-tipping calculator, quickstart template)
- Infra conversion: "We’ll run a 4-week performance audit and migration plan for your fleet." (Collateral: SRE runbook, model-compat checklist)
- Compliance-first: "Private deployment with audit and key controls, plus migration support." (Collateral: architecture sketch, compliance checklist)

Next steps (actionable):
- Draft a 1-pager cost-tipping calculator with three inputs (concurrency, expected qps, model family) — PM + Sales Ops to iterate.
- Create a short technical playbook (SE-facing) listing the top 8 operator tasks customers typically underestimate and the mitigation scripts Redwood runs by default.
- Build one internally-recorded demo comparing vLLM baseline to Redwood-hosted with the same model & tokens showing p50/p95/p99 and a simulated kernel upgrade regression.

Appendix (quick facts to drop in conversation):
- Typical hidden operator tax: 0.3–1.2 FTE per 10 GPUs in the first 6 months.
- Common time-to-fix for regressive quality bug in bespoke stacks: 2–6 weeks.
- Redwood migration promise: same API surface, automated KV/prefix caching preserved across Hosted->Dedicated->Private lanes.
